$comment: This file is the authored source and is not generated. scripts/build-tokens.mts reads this file and emits app/tokens.generated.css and lib/generated/tokens.ts.

cssNaming.$comment: Rungs are addressed by NAME, not by number: --opsin-material-sheet-blur, not --opsin-material-3-blur. A number invites arithmetic ('one more than a card') and the ladder is not arithmetic. Each rung answers a different question about what is behind it.

rules: A material is a decision about what is behind the surface, not a decoration. Pick the rung by asking what the reader needs to keep seeing through it.

Every translucent rung declares a MINIMUM scrim opacity and an OPAQUE fallback, and text on it is measured against the worst case, not against the average backdrop. A contrast floor that holds only over a light photograph is not a floor.

At most three composited translucent surfaces may be stacked. Beyond three the blur cost is visible on the mid-range Android devices this system targets, and the fourth layer's backdrop is already unreadable.
`prefers-reduced-transparency` is honoured by swapping to `opaqueFallback`, not by removing the surface. The layering still has to communicate.
Never place a health value on a translucent rung above `raised`. A number a reader is trying to read must not sit over a moving backdrop.

ladder.name: canvas
ladder.question: What is the page itself?
ladder.use: The application background. Nothing is behind it, so nothing shows through it.

ladder.name: inset
ladder.question: Is this a recess carved into a card, not a surface lifted above it?
ladder.use: The recessed well inside a card: the explanatory note a Callout draws inside the reading it annotates, and the track a RangeBar lays its range along. Its fill sits below the card fill in both themes, so the well reads as carved into the card rather than lifted off it. In light it is neutral-100, one step under the white card, which is where a Callout already sat. In dark it is a value between the page and the card, below the card so the well is a recess and above the page so a Callout used on its own is still visible.
ladder.note: A token-only rung. Its half-step number says it sits between canvas and card without renumbering the six named rungs the ladder documents and Surface exposes. Callout and RangeBar read --opsin-material-inset-tint directly; Surface's rung prop and the MaterialRung union stay at the six elevation rungs, because a recess is not a thing a reader raises a Surface to. The dark tint and opaqueFallback are the one entry in this ladder authored as a raw oklch rather than a --opsin-neutral-* name, because the neutral ramp holds no step between neutral-900 at L 0.205 and neutral-950 at L 0.145, and the recess needs L 0.178, between the dark card fill and the dark page. build-tokens.mts emits this rung as a literal rather than a var() reference, so unlike every other rung it does not follow a re-tune of the neutral ramp: if the ramp is re-tuned, either add a neutral step near L 0.178 and name it here, or re-pick this literal by hand so the recess still sits between the dark card and the dark page.

ladder.name: card
ladder.question: Is this a distinct piece of content on the page?
ladder.use: The default home for a health value. Opaque, bounded by a line rather than a shadow, and the rung every ResultCard, MetricTile and RangeBar sits on.
ladder.note: Deliberately shadowless. A grid of shadowed cards on a phone reads as clutter, and the shadow is doing work a 1px boundary does better and cheaper.

ladder.name: raised
ladder.question: Is this temporarily above the page, but not covering it?
ladder.use: Menus, popovers, tooltips, a dragged card. Still opaque: the shadow, not translucency, is what says 'above'.
ladder.note: This is the highest rung a health value may sit on.

ladder.name: sheet
ladder.question: Is this covering the page while leaving it recognisable underneath?
ladder.$comment: minScrimOpacity is published once per rung, but tintAlpha is published per theme, and the component renders each theme at max(tintAlpha, minScrimOpacity). The dark tintAlpha here (0.90) sits below the floor (0.93), so max() returns the floor and the authored dark alpha never renders. A dark tintAlpha may not be set below minScrimOpacity and be expected to take effect. To make a lower dark alpha effective, publish minScrimOpacity per theme, which is a build-tokens change.
ladder.use: A bottom sheet or side panel the reader can dismiss by dragging. Its tint is now near opaque, so the panel lands close to the card colour and a white control inside it no longer floats above a greyer surface. What keeps the covered page recognisable is the scrim around the panel rather than the page reading through the panel, because at this opacity very little of the page shows through the tint.
ladder.note: The rung stays translucent rather than becoming a fourth opaque rung for two reasons. prefers-reduced-transparency and print still swap it to its opaque fallback, so it needs one declared. And the thin translucency it keeps still carries the saturation boost. The dark tint is a declared 0.90 that the published floor raises to 0.93, the same floor the light tint already meets, so both themes render the panel at roughly the same opacity. Saturation is boosted above 1 because a large blur desaturates whatever is behind it, and without the boost the sheet looks grey rather than translucent.

ladder.name: overlay
ladder.question: Is this chrome floating over scrolling content?
ladder.$comment: minScrimOpacity is published once per rung, but tintAlpha is published per theme, and the component renders each theme at max(tintAlpha, minScrimOpacity). The dark tintAlpha here (0.7) sits below the floor (0.74), so max() returns the floor and the authored dark alpha never renders. A dark tintAlpha may not be set below minScrimOpacity and be expected to take effect. To make a lower dark alpha effective, publish minScrimOpacity per theme, which is a build-tokens change.
ladder.use: A pinned toolbar, a tab bar and a floating action bar are all chrome that content scrolls beneath.
ladder.note: The thinnest material in the system, and therefore the one whose contrast floor is hardest to hold. Anything on it is measured against the darkest and the lightest backdrop the product can produce, not against the tint alone.

ladder.name: scrim
ladder.question: Am I trying to make everything behind this unusable on purpose?
ladder.use: The dimming layer behind a modal dialog or a consent sheet. Its job is to remove the page from consideration, not to look like glass.
ladder.note: The only rung that gets darker rather than lighter, and the only one whose blur is deliberately tiny: a heavy blur here turns the page behind into an attractive abstract texture, which is the opposite of the intent.

budget.$comment: Counted as the number of simultaneously visible rungs with translucent: true. A sheet over a scrim over a page is three and is the designed worst case. A popover on a sheet on a scrim is four and must be redesigned, not tuned.

reducedTransparency.policy: Every rung with translucent: true swaps its tint for its opaqueFallback and drops its blur to 0. Nothing else changes: the border, the shadow and the geometry stay, because they are what carry the layering once the translucency is gone.
reducedTransparency.$comment: This is also the fallback for browsers with no backdrop-filter support, so the query and the @supports fallback emit the same declarations. See /docs/foundations/materials/reduced-transparency.

contrastFloor.$comment: The published APCA and WCAG numbers for text on a material are its worst case, and that worst case is produced one way for an opaque rung and another for a translucent one. For an opaque rung the surface the reader sees is the tint itself, so that is what the text is measured against. For a translucent rung the surface the reader sees is the tint composited at its own tintAlpha over whatever is behind it, so the text is measured against the tint composited over both backdrops named above, the darkest and the lightest the product can produce, and the worse of the two figures is published. The opaque fallback is not the worst case for a translucent rung. A light tint over dark scrolling content is at its lightest, and so at its kindest to dark text, exactly when the opaque fallback is the fill, so measuring against the fallback alone would publish the flattering figure rather than the honest one. This is what the overlay rung's note has always demanded. scripts/check-contrast.mts implements the composite and lib/generated/contrast.json records the result. Exactly one contrast floor is published per rung, and none is published for large text. A large-text floor is a separate measurement, not a relaxation that can be assumed from the body floor. Any component prop that selects between a body floor and a large-text floor ships in the same commit as the token that gives it an effect, and never before, so a prop cannot promise a floor these tokens do not yet publish.
